activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: At an airport, families wait in the arrivals area to meet people coming off a plane.
story:
Maeva and Dad went to the airport. Grandma was coming on a plane. "We wait here," said Dad. "This is the arrivals area. Families wait here to meet people coming off a plane." The doors opened. A tall man came out. "Grandma!" Maeva would yell. But it was not Grandma. A lady with a red hat came out. Not Grandma either. Then the doors opened one more time. Grandma! She hugged Maeva so tight.

The next day they all went to the park. Grandma brought a kite in her bag. That was a surprise. Maeva held the string and ran. The wind caught the kite. The kite went up and up. It flew far over the trees. "I did it!" Maeva would yell. Grandma laughed and clapped.

At the picnic table, Dad cut the bread. He made warm sandwiches for everyone. Maeva took a big bite. "Best picnic ever," said Grandma. The kite danced in the sky above them.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The rhyme 'One, Two, Buckle My Shoe' puts the counting words into a rhyme.
story:
Paisley sat on the blue rug at daycare. Miss Jo held up ten paper shoes. "Let's count them," she said. Tom started. "One, two..." Then he stopped. His face went red. "I forgot what comes next."

Miss Jo smiled. "Try the shoe song," she said. She sang it. "One, two, buckle my shoe."

Tom sang with her. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door!" He clapped his hands. "It rhymes! The words rhyme together!"

Paisley wanted to try too. "Three, four, shut the door," she sang. The words felt bouncy in her mouth, like a joke that tickled. "Five, six, pick up sticks."

Tom picked up a crayon from the floor. "Look! I picked up a stick!" Everyone laughed. Then they all sang more. "Seven, eight, lay them straight." They laid ten crayons in a neat row on the rug.

Paisley could see the row of shoes and the row of crayons. She counted them all by herself. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

Tom patted her arm. "You did it," he said. Paisley sang the last part softly. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen."

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: You can often tell how a friend feels by looking at their face.
story:
Julia put on her soft pajama shirt. It was bedtime, but her teddy bear looked sad. His mouth was turned down in a frown. "Are you sad, Bear?" she asked. She gave him a hug. Bear's face felt better after that.

Then Bunny came along. Bunny's eyes were wide and her mouth was open. "You look scared," said Julia. So Julia tucked Bunny under her sweet blue blanket. Bunny stopped shaking. Julia smiled a big smile. She was happy now too.

Dino stomped in with a big frown and grumpy eyebrows. "You look angry, Dino," said Julia. She stuck one sticker on his nose. It was a star sticker. Dino's frown turned into a grin. Julia yawned. She tucked everyone into bed. "Goodnight, friends," she said. Then she closed her eyes and dreamed of stars.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Chocolate can make dogs very sick, so dogs are never given chocolate.
story:
Jack walked home with Dad. He held the leash in both hands. His new dog, Bella, trotted beside him. She had a shiny black nose and a wagging tail.

Jack had a chocolate treat in his pocket. He took it out. "Treat for you, Bella!" he said. Dad stopped him gently. "No, Jack. Chocolate can make dogs very sick. Dogs are never given chocolate." Jack looked at his treat. Then he looked at Bella. He felt worried.

Dad reached into his bag. "You can give her this instead." It was a dog treat, shaped like a little bone. Jack held it out on his flat hand. Bella took it softly. She wagged her tail fast. A bird began to sing above them. "Good dog," Jack said. Bella licked his cheek. Jack laughed and held her leash tight all the way home.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use.
story:
Jacob ran to the big backyard. Grandpa was there by the grill. The grill was hot, so Jacob stayed back. He could hear the food sizzle.

Jacob saw something small on the grass. It was brown and shiny. It had a little flame button on it. It was a lighter. Jacob wanted to pick it up. But he did not. He stopped his hand.

"Grandpa, I found something!" Jacob called. Grandpa came right away. He picked up the lighter. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use," said Grandpa. He put it in his pocket, far up high.

Then Grandpa said, "The food is ready. We can share it together." They sat at the brown picnic table. Jacob ate a warm bun. Grandpa gave him a cool cup of water. "Hot and cold," said Jacob, touching the cup with both hands. Grandpa smiled and held Jacob's hand.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: We ask before we take something that belongs to someone else.
story:
Charles sat at the dinner table. His sister Mia had a shiny red apple. Charles wanted it very much.

He reached across the table. He grabbed the apple quick. Mia's face went sad. "That is mine," she said. She did not laugh. She looked like she might cry.

Charles put the apple back on her plate. He thought hard. "Can I have the apple, please?" he asked. Mia smiled a big smile. "Yes! We can share it." Their mom cut the apple in two. Half for Charles. Half for Mia. Mom poured milk for each of them too. The milk was cold and sweet.

"Can I have your paint tomorrow?" Charles asked Mia. "Yes, if you ask," said Mia. "Ask, ask, ask," said Charles. Dad laughed. "That is the way."

The apple was crunchy. Charles ate his half slow. Mia ate her half too. After dinner, Charles felt warm and happy. His tummy was full. Then he yawned. Soon his eyes closed and he fell asleep in his chair.

Mom picked him up. "My big boy," she said softly. "He asked."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Teammates can cheer for each other, even when someone misses.
story:
Brooks was at the big pool. His swim team was playing a game. They had to push a ball across the water. Brooks wore his red cap. His friend Mia held a rubber sheep. The sheep could float. They let it hide under a snowy white towel before the game.

The coach blew the whistle. Brooks kicked hard. The ball came to him. He pushed. The ball went past his hands. It missed the goal. Brooks felt his face go hot.

But then his team began to cheer. "Try again, Brooks! You can do it!" they called. Mia waved the sheep. The ball came back. Brooks pushed it again. This time it went in. The team splashed and cheered louder. "Good try, good try, good try," they sang. Brooks laughed and splashed back at them.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: In Japan, people say 'itadakimasu' before eating to give thanks for the food.
story:
Aiden ran into the big hall. His boots went clomp, clomp on the floor. There were tables everywhere. Grandpa was there too.

"Big dinner tonight," said Grandpa. "We say a special word first."

"Say it with me," said Grandpa. "Itadakimasu."

"Eeta... ducky... moo?" said Aiden.

Grandpa laughed. "Close! Try again."

Aiden took a big breath. "Itadakimasu!"

"Now we can eat," said Grandpa. He picked up his spoon.

Aiden looked at the rice. He said the word again. "Itadakimasu!" Then he ate a big bite.

"You said it just right," said Grandpa. "That's the true word for before we eat."

Aiden clomped his boots under the table. He was happy. He had rice on his nose.

"Grandpa, do we need more rice?" he asked.

Grandpa grinned. "Maybe just one more bowl."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Glasses help some people see more clearly.
story:
Kayden wanted Grandpa to read his book. But Grandpa could not find the words on the page.

Kayden used his eyes to look. He used his ears to listen. Where were the glasses? He touched the soft couch. He touched the cold table. "Two, three, four places," he counted.

Then Kayden smelled toast with his nose. He followed the smelly, warm smell to the kitchen. Grandma was there. "Do you remember winter?" she asked. "You wore mittens so your hands stayed warm." She handed Grandpa his glasses from the counter.

Grandpa put on his glasses. He opened the book. Now he could see the words. He read the story to Kayden.

"The glasses help me see more clearly," Grandpa said.

Kayden tasted the sweet toast. He clapped his hands. "Again," he said. "Read it again, Grandpa."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: In and out are opposites.
story:
Blake was at daycare. She wanted to build a big tower. She put a block in the box, then took it out again.

Baby Sam crawled over. Sam put toys in the box. Blake took them out. Sam put them in. Blake laughed.

"You two," said Miss Kim. "In and out are opposites."

Blake tried it herself. Block in. Block out. In, out, in, out. Sam clapped his small hands.

Then Blake made her tower. It was big. It grew fast. Sam knocked it down, slow and soft, with one little push. Blake did not cry. She built it again.

At snack time, Miss Kim gave out warm muffins. "Careful, they're hot," she said. Blake blew on hers. Then she drank her cold milk.

Sam pointed at the box. "Da," he said.

Blake put a ball in the box. Sam pulled it out. They played the game until it was time to go home.

"Bye, Sam," said Blake. "You are not alone. I will sit by you tomorrow."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: The author is the person who wrote the words of a book.
story:
Theodore went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about spiders. He found a green book with a big spider on the cover. He opened it at the back. The pages felt funny that way. The words ran the wrong way. He turned the book around. He began at the front. Now the spider story started right. One spider, two spiders, three spiders on a web.

"Mom, who made up this spider story?" Theodore asked.

Mom took him to the librarian. The librarian pointed to the cover. She put her finger on a name. "This is the author," she said. "The author is the person who wrote the words of the book." Theodore looked at the name. It said Anna Lee. So Anna Lee wrote the words. Every page, all the spider words.

Theodore held the book tight. He found another book by Anna Lee. It had a bear asleep in a cave. He carried both books to the desk. "These are Anna Lee's words," he told the librarian. She smiled and stamped the books. Theodore counted them out loud. "One book, two books." Then he sat by the window and turned to page one.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Two people can feel differently about the same thing.
story:
Clara ran to the music corner at school. She was so excited. A big purple drum sat on the rug. Clara hit it with her hands. Boom! Boom! The sound was loud and fun. Clara laughed and laughed.

Then she saw her friend Ben. He was sad. He had his hands over his ears. "Too loud," Ben said. His face looked scared. Clara stopped drumming. She felt confused. She loved the drum. But Ben did not love it. She thought and thought. The same drum, but two different feelings!

Clara looked around the room. She found a box of magnets on the shelf. She held one up. "Want to play magnets, Ben?" she asked. Ben took his hands off his ears. He smiled a big smile. He was happy now. The magnets clicked together. They filled the whole rug with click, click, click sounds.

Miss Maya came over. "What a quiet game," she said. Then came a small surprise. The magnet stuck to the drum. Clara gasped. "Look, Ben! The magnet likes your drum too." Ben tapped the drum very, very soft. Tap. Tap. "I like it now," Ben said.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: On the school bus, children stay sitting in their seats.
story:
Sofia stood in the school hallway. It was her very first day. She held her red backpack with both hands.

The hallway had a big window. Sofia looked out. She could see the school bus parked by the door.

A boy got on the bus. He waved and waved at Sofia. Then he stood up in his seat to wave more. The driver turned around. "Sit down, please," the driver said. "On the school bus, children stay sitting in their seats."

The boy sat down. Then he waved from his seat instead. Sofia waved back. His hand went left and right through the window glass. She saw that sitting down still let him wave. "Look at that," Sofia whispered.

A girl named Mia walked up next to her. "Do you see the bus too?" Mia asked.

"Yes," said Sofia. "The boy sits and waves. He does not stand. What else can you see from here?"

Mia pointed at the field. "Sheep!" she said. Two white sheep stood by the fence. One sheep walked to the other sheep.

Sofia clapped her hands. Then the teacher called, "Line up, everyone!"

Sofia and Mia got in line. Sofia turned for one more look. The bus doors closed with a big whoosh, and off it went down the road.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: A cup with nothing in it is empty, and a cup filled to the top is full.
story:
John sat in his big car seat. The car went fast. "Slow down, Daddy," said Mommy. Daddy drove slow by the cows. The cows were big. The birds were small.

John was hungry. Mommy had a cup of cold juice. John took a sip. The cup was not full now. Soon the cup was empty. "All gone," said John.

Then Daddy stopped the car. Daddy got a thermos of hot soup, but Daddy held it himself. "It's hot, so I pour," said Daddy. Daddy poured some soup into a clean cup. He poured too fast and the cup got too full. Some soup spilled. Daddy wiped it up with a napkin. Then Daddy poured slow. He stopped before the top. "This cup is full," said Daddy. "It is not empty."

John held his cup with two hands. He looked inside. The soup went all the way up. John smiled at Daddy and took a tiny sip.

"Wag your tail," John said to the dog in the next car, whose bone sat on the seat.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Covering different holes on a recorder makes different notes.
story:
Maya ran into the garage. Dad had a surprise in his bag. It was a little flute called a recorder! "I want to play it now," said Maya. Dad showed her the holes on top. "Put your fingers on the holes," he said.

Maya blew into the recorder. It went squeak! That was not a nice sound. She looked down. One finger was not covering its hole all the way. She pressed her finger flat and hard on the hole. She blew again. Out came a real note! "Dad, listen!" she said.

Then Maya lifted one finger. The note changed! She put the finger back. The note went back. She lifted another finger. A new note came out. Maya played up and down, up and down. Dad tapped his foot. "Play it again!" he said. Maya smiled and blew a long, happy note.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In baseball, the batter wears a helmet to protect their head.
story:
Zayn ran to the bat. One, two, three, swing time! "Hold on, Zayn," said Coach Ben. "You need your helmet first."

Zayn stopped. He touched his head. "Why?" he asked.

"The batter wears a helmet to protect the head," said Coach Ben. He set the blue helmet on Zayn. It felt big and a little cold at first.

Zayn looked around. Every batter had a helmet. Mia had one. Sam had one. One, two, three helmets on the bench!

Zayn stood at the plate. He gave a little wave to his mom. Then the ball came. Zayn swung. Ping! The ball flew far. It went over the grass and began to fall down, down, down near second base.

"Run, Zayn, run!" his team called. Zayn ran, and his helmet stayed on tight the whole way.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In soccer, players try to get the ball into the net to score a goal.
story:
William was on the swim team this summer. Every morning he went to the big pool. Coach Sam had a fun game for the team today.

At the small end of the pool, Coach Sam put a floating net in the water. Then he dropped a beach ball next to William. "In soccer, we try to get the ball into the net," said Coach Sam. "We play soccer in the water today!"

William pushed the ball with his hands. The ball bobbed away. It went past the net. It did not go in. Mia, on his team, splashed and pushed it back to him.

William tried a new way. He kicked the ball with his foot under the water. Kick, kick, kick. The big splash made the ball roll. It rolled and rolled. It rolled right into the net!

"Goal!" everyone shouted. Mia clapped her hands. Coach Sam blew his whistle. William laughed and jumped up and down. The water went splash on his nose.

"Now you kick it to me!" said Mia. William lined up the ball with his foot. He gave it a big kick. "Here it comes!"

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: A library card lets you borrow books and take them home to read.
story:
Lily sat in the little reading corner. A soft rug was under her feet. Books sat on low shelves all around. She found a big red book. It had a dragon on the cover. The dragon had fire coming out of its mouth.

"I love this one," said Lily. She hugged the book. It felt rough on the cover. But books had to stay at the library. Lily's face went sad.

The librarian came over. She smiled. "Would you like a library card?" she asked.

"A card for me?" said Lily. "Yes!" So Lily wrote her name. The librarian made a shiny new card.

The librarian laughed. "Your card lets you borrow books. You can take them home to read."

"Home? This book can come home with ME?" Lily hugged the dragon book again. She put it in her bag. The bag had a strap that would hang on her hook at home.

At bedtime, Lily read about the dragon. It blew fire at a big hill of socks. "Silly dragon," said Lily. She patted the book. "You live at the library. But tonight you sleep here."

She put the book by her pillow. "Night night, dragon," she whispered.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Saying 'excuse me' is a polite way to get past someone who is in your way.
story:
Ethan stood at the door of his class. A big dragon was blocking the way. It was really Ben in a green dragon costume, and Ben was very still.

Ethan wanted to get past. He tried to squeeze by. The dragon wiggled and did not move. Ethan almost fell.

Then Miss Ana came close. "Say excuse me," she said in a gentle voice.

"Excuse me, dragon," said Ethan.

The dragon turned his head. He stepped to the side with a swish of his tail. The way was open now.

"Thank you, dragon," said Ethan.

The dragon bowed. "Excuse me is how a knight gets past a dragon," said the dragon.

Ethan walked through the door. He felt like a real knight with a shiny sword. At the craft table he picked up the glue.

"Please can I have the blue paper?" he asked. The teacher smiled and gave him two pieces. He made a tall, tall castle with a flag on top.

At home time, Ben fell down and did not cry. Ethan helped him up.

"Sorry I bumped you," said Ben.

"That's okay," said Ethan.

They marched out together, two knights side by side.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your fingertips can tell if something is soft, rough, smooth or bumpy.
story:
Colton ran to the play table at daycare. Miss Ana had a big box. "It is a guessing game," she said. "Close your eyes."

Colton shut his eyes tight. He could not see anything. But he could hear Miss Ana shake the box. Rattle, rattle!

"Now touch," said Miss Ana. Colton put his fingertips on something. It felt bumpy all over. His fingertips knew it! "A pinecone!" he said. He opened his eyes. Yes! It was a pinecone.

Next he felt something soft. Soft like a baby duck. "A feather!" he said. He was right again. Then he touched something smooth. Smooth and cool. "A rock!" It was a smooth stone.

The kids smelled snack next. Colton's nose sniffed warm apples. He could taste the sweet apple too. Yum!

Later, Miss Ana gave him paint. Colton made a messy picture with his hands. "Feel this!" he said to his friend. "Bumpy paint!"

His friend touched it and laughed. "Bumpy!" said his friend.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: You can show how old you are by holding up that many fingers.
story:
Today was Ellie's birthday party in her classroom. There was a cake on the table. There were cups and plates. On the wall, a big paper owl would hang over the party. Ellie held it up high. "I will hang you, owl," she said. The owl hung there and looked down at everyone.

A new boy named Sam came in. He had never met Ellie before. "How old are you?" Sam asked. Ellie held up her fingers. She counted them. "One, two, three," she said. Sam laughed. "Three? But your mom said four!" Ellie looked at her hand. One finger was hiding down low. She lifted it up. "One, two, three, four!" she said. "I am four!" She wiggled the four fingers. Sam held up four fingers too. "I am four also!" he said.

Then Ellie went around the room. She asked her grandma. Grandma held up six fingers, and everyone laughed. She asked her friend Mia. Mia held up three fingers. Ellie looked everywhere for one more cup. The pink cup was lost! It was under the chair. Ellie found it and put it on the table. Then everyone sang. Ellie blew out the candles with a big puff. "Happy birthday, Ellie!" they all said. Sam waved four fingers at her and grinned.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When you feel excited, you might want to jump, bounce or shout.
story:
Lucy was at the park with her mama. Grandma was coming to visit. Lucy wanted to see Grandma so much. She felt excited. When she felt excited, her legs wanted to bounce. They boing, boing, boinged. Her mouth wanted to shout. "Grandma! Grandma!"

But Grandma was not there yet. Lucy looked down the path. She saw a boy near the swings. He was crying. He felt sad. His kite was stuck in a tree. "I can help," Lucy said. She waited while Mama got the kite down. The boy stopped crying. He smiled a big smile.

Lucy heard a loud dog bark. She felt scared. She held Mama's hand. The dog ran past. It did not stop. Lucy let out her breath. She was not scared anymore.

Then Lucy saw a red balloon floating away. She felt angry. "Come back, balloon!" she said. But the balloon went up, up, up. Then, surprise! The wind blew it back down. It landed right in Lucy's hands. She laughed.

Lucy's legs began to bounce again. Boing, boing, boing. She took a big breath. She sat on the bench. She counted the clouds. One, two, three. Then she heard a voice. "Hello, my Lucy!" It was Grandma! Lucy ran with the red balloon. Grandma opened her arms wide.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: At a concert, people in the audience clap when the music is over to show they enjoyed it.
story:
Everly sat in the big red seat. Her mama sat next to her. The stage had many chairs and shiny horns. A woman began to play a quiet song on a violin.

Everly wanted to clap. She lifted her hands. Then she looked around. Nobody else was clapping. Everyone sat still and quiet. So Everly kept her hands in her lap. She waited.

The music went on and on. Everly tapped her toes. The toe taps matched the beat, tap, tap, tap. She played the toe game in her shoes. She hummed her nursery rhyme inside her head. Twinkle, twinkle, little star. She sang it to herself, all the way to the end.

At last the music stopped. The violin came down. Then everyone clapped at once. Clap, clap, clap! Everly clapped too, loud and fast. A lady in front turned and smiled at her.

Later they sat in the lobby. Everly ate a salty pretzel from the snack table. "Next song, I will wait," Everly said. "Then I will clap and show I liked it." She took another big bite of her pretzel.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: A pencil needs sharpening when its tip gets dull, and a grown-up can help.
story:
Nathan sat at the big table in writing club. He had a red hat on his head. He wanted to write his name. Miss Ana gave him a pencil. Nathan held it in his fist. The letters came out big and wobbly. Then his pencil made a fat, fuzzy line. The line was wide and soft, not sharp at all.

"Why is my line so fuzzy?" Nathan asked. Miss Ana looked at the pencil. "The tip is dull," she said. "Can you fix it?" asked Nathan. Miss Ana took the pencil to the sharpener. She turned it round and round. Grown-ups did the sharp part. Nathan waited with his hands in his lap.

Miss Ana gave the pencil back. The tip was pointy now. Nathan held it with his fingers, nice and easy. He drew the N. The line was thin and dark. Then A, then T, then H. "Nathan!" he read out loud. His friend Sam leaned over. "Your N looks like a little hat!" Nathan laughed and made one more N, just to see it again.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Each team wears its own colors so you can tell the two teams apart.
story:
Margot sat on the couch with Dad. The big game was on TV. Uncle Ben was there too. Everyone was shouting and clapping.

Margot watched the players run. She could not tell them apart. "Dad, which team is which?" she asked. "Look at the shirts," said Dad. "Each team wears its own colors. The red team is ours. The blue team is the other team." Margot looked hard. Red shirts ran one way. Blue shirts ran the other way. Now she could see them! "Red team, go!" she shouted. A red player kicked the ball. Goal!

"Can I wear red too?" Margot asked. "Yes," said Uncle Ben. He hurried to get his red scarf. He wrapped it around her neck. It was soft and warm. Margot snuggled under the blanket with Dad. Her legs were cozy. The dog was lazy on the rug. The red team ran down the field again. "Go, go, go!" said Margot. Dad gave her a high five. "That one was ours," said Margot. "I can tell now."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Seeds need water to start growing, and a sprout does not come up right away.
story:
Jordan dug a deep hole in the school garden. His teacher, Miss Ana, gave him three little seeds. "These are carrot seeds," she said. Jordan put the seeds in the hole. He patted the dirt down with his hands.

Then Jordan got the watering can. He tipped it over the dirt. Water dripped down, dark and wet. "Seeds need water to start growing," said Miss Ana. Jordan shared the watering can with his friend Milo. They watered the seeds together.

The next morning, Jordan ran to the garden. He looked and looked. There was only dirt. No sprout yet. Jordan watered the seeds again. He waited one more day. He watered them again. On the third day, Jordan saw something small and green. A sprout! He jumped up and down. "Milo, come see!" he called.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: A book in English starts at the front cover, and you turn the pages until you reach the back.
story:
Ethan wanted a story before bed. He ran to get his book. But he could not find his mom. He waited on the bed and hugged the book.

He opened the book by himself. He started at the back. He turned a page. The picture showed a dog at the end of a long day. On the next page, the dog was already home. "That is all mixed up," Ethan said. The dog barked in one picture. Then it slept. Then it played. It made no sense at all.

Mom came in. "Ready for your story?" she asked. Ethan held up the book. "It is all mixed up," he said. Mom smiled. "Try the other way," she said. Ethan flipped the book over. Now he held the front cover. He turned the pages one by one. First the dog woke up. Then it barked at a cat. Then it went home. Then it slept. The story went the right way, all the way to the back cover.

Ethan snuggled down under his blanket. "The front is the start," he said. Mom kissed his head. "Good night, Ethan," she said. Ethan closed the book and patted the front cover.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: A library puts its books on shelves in groups so people can find them.
story:
William jumped into the car seat. "Library time!" he shouted.

Daddy started the car. William looked out the window. He saw a dog. He saw a cow. "Animals everywhere!" he said.

At the library, William ran to a big shelf. He wanted a book about animals. He looked and looked. He saw books about trucks. He saw books about food, with apples on them. No animal books. Where were they? His animal book felt missing.

A librarian came to help. "Follow me," she said. She pointed to a shelf. All the animal books sat there together. Birds, bears, and one big elephant on the cover.

"The animal books live in a group," she said.

William reached for the elephant book. He hugged it tight.

Back in the car, he held it on his lap. At home, he drew an elephant with his gray crayon. "Big ears!" he said.

Daddy laughed. "Let's read it again."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange.
story:
Michael was at Grandma's house. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. He looked in the paint box. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was no orange paint.

"I need orange," said Michael. "The pumpkin is orange." Grandma smiled. "Let's see what we can do," she said. Michael dipped his brush in the red paint. He put red on the pumpkin. Then he dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He put yellow on top of the red.

The brush went round and round. The red paint mixed with the yellow paint. The pumpkin turned orange! Michael touched the paint with his finger. It felt slimy. "Look, Grandma!" he said. "Red and yellow made orange!" Grandma laughed softly. Michael picked up his pumpkin. He held it up to the window. "It looks just like a real one," he said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Morning is the part of the day when we wake up and eat breakfast.
story:
Madelyn woke up in her little bed. The sun was bright in her window. She heard spoons and cups in the kitchen. She ran down the hall. Mama, Papa, and Baby Sam were at the table. There were eggs and toast and milk. "Good morning," said Mama. "Good morning," said Madelyn. She sat down and ate her toast.

Yesterday Madelyn had wanted to plant seeds. Papa had said, "Not now. Later." Today she asked again. "Can we plant the seeds today?" "We can," said Papa. "First we eat breakfast. Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast. Then we go outside." Madelyn ate two eggs. She drank all her milk.

Then Papa got the seed packet. Madelyn dropped three seeds into her hand. They went out to the big pot by the door. The dirt was soft and cool. Madelyn pushed each seed down with one finger. One seed got stuck to her thumb. She shook her hand and it fell in. Papa gave her water in a small cup. She poured it on the dirt.

"Now the seeds stay in the dirt," said Papa. "Tomorrow we will look at the pot. Tomorrow is the day after today." Madelyn patted the dirt. "Good night, seeds," she said. "See you tomorrow." The pot sat still and quiet in the sun.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice.
story:
Hailey was at Grandpa's house. She wanted to show Grandpa her new red ball. She ran down the hall. "Grandpa!" she shouted.

Mama put her hand up soft. "The baby is sleeping," she whispered. "We use a quiet voice."

Hailey looked at the baby. The baby's eyes were closed. Hailey made her voice very small. "Grandpa," she whispered.

Grandpa smiled and whispered back, "Hello, Hailey." They rolled the red ball to each other on the rug. The ball went tap, tap, so soft. Grandpa rolled it to Hailey. Then Hailey rolled it to Grandpa. They took turns, back and forth.

Outside, a truck rumbled by on the street. Hailey covered her mouth. But the baby still slept.

Then the baby woke up. She was not sad. She made a happy sound. Hailey held up her ball and whispered, "My turn, baby. You can share."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Heavy and light are opposites.
story:
Carter wants to build a big tower at daycare. He finds a heavy box. He pulls and pulls. The box does not move. It is too heavy.

His friend Mia has a pillow. It is light. Carter lifts it up high. It is easy! "Look," says Mia. "Heavy and light are opposites." Carter puts the pillow on top of the box. The tower grows, one soft pillow at a time.

Now Carter wants a faster tower. He runs to get more pillows. Then he stops. He goes slow and careful. The pillows stay on top. The tower stands tall. Teacher Sam brings warm cocoa in little cups. "Hot," says Teacher Sam. "Blow first." Carter blows. He sips. "Cold now!" The tower is big. Carter is small. But his tower is the tallest in the room. "Again tomorrow," says Carter.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A plant's roots grow down into the soil.
story:
Blake went to the garden center with Dad. She wanted to plant a little garden. Blake picked carrot seeds and pea seeds. She held the seed packets tight.

At home, Dad helped her dig in the dirt. Blake dropped the seeds in. She patted the soil down. Then she watered it with her small blue can.

One day a green weed grew near her peas. Blake pulled it, gently, gently. Out it came. Long stringy roots hung from the bottom! "Wow," said Blake. "The roots grow down into the soil!" Dad laughed. "Yes, they do." Blake patted the soil back down. Her pea plant stayed snug, roots down below, growing and growing.

Soon the peas were tall. Blake picked one and had a taste. "Sweet!" she said. Dad had a taste too. "Mmm," he said. "My peas win the number one prize." Blake giggled and picked one more.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Today is the day that is happening right now.
story:
Matteo pulled his blanket up to his chin. "Mom," he said, "is today the library day?"

Mom sat on the bed. Her face was soft in the lamp light. "Yes," she said. "Today is the day that is happening right now. And we went today."

Matteo thought hard. He remembered the morning. He had picked three books. He had hugged them all the way home. That was today.

"But I want to go again," he said. "Can we go now?"

Mom shook her head gently. "Now it is bedtime. The library is closed. You can go later."

"How long is later?" asked Matteo.

"Later comes after you sleep," said Mom. "When you wake up, it will be tomorrow. Tomorrow we can read your new books."

Matteo looked at the books by his pillow. Yesterday he had no books. Today he had three. Tomorrow he would open the first one.

"The sun went away today," said Mom. "Now it is dark. The snow will fall while you sleep."

Matteo snuggled down. His blanket felt warm. "Today was a good day," he said.

"Yes," said Mom. "And tomorrow is coming soon."

She kissed his cheek. Matteo closed his eyes.

"Read to me tomorrow," he whispered. "The bear book first."

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: Rinsing under the water washes the soap off your hands.
story:
Harper went to the pharmacy with her dad. She had to use the toilet. After that, they went to the little sink. Dad put soap on her hands. "We count to twenty," said Dad. Harper rubbed and rubbed. "Ten, eleven, twelve," she said. Her hands felt slippery.

Then Dad turned on the water. The water ran over Harper's hands. The slippery feeling went away. "Where did the soap go?" she asked. "The water washed it off," said Dad. Harper held up her hands. "My hands are not slippery now!" she said. "Slippery gone, slippery gone," she sang.

A small boy pointed at the sink. "My turn," he said. His mom helped him wash. Harper gave him a quick wave. "Count to twenty," she told him. On the way out, Dad bought a bandage for his knee. Harper carried the little bag all the way home.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Freshly fallen snow is white.
story:
Gabriel rode his bike to Grandma's house. Snow fell from the sky. It fell on the grass. It fell on Grandma's red door. Gabriel looked down. "The snow is white," he said. All the snow was white.

Gabriel wanted to draw the snow. He got white paper. He got a white crayon. He drew and drew. But nothing showed up! White on white was invisible. Grandma gave him a hug. "Try again," she said. Gabriel looked at the paper stack. He picked the blue paper. He drew white snow on it. Now the snow showed up! White on blue was easy to see.

Gabriel added a yellow sun. He added a green tree. Grandma made hot cocoa, and she chewed a peppermint while he drew. Then Gabriel saw a surprise. Outside, a red bird sat on the white snow. It looked just like his yellow sun on blue sky. He drew it fast. "Snowy red bird," he said.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Wet paint can smudge if you touch it.
story:
Eliana went to the art gallery with her papa. There was a painting of a big red monkey. Eliana touched the monkey's tail. Her finger left a smudge on the wet paint. "Oh no," said Eliana. A kind woman said, "The paint is still wet. It can smudge if you touch it." Eliana looked at her fingerprint in the tail.

Then the woman took Eliana to a little table. There were three pots of paint. "This one is red," said the woman. "This one is blue. This one is yellow." Eliana said the names out loud. "Red. Blue. Yellow." She said them again, like a song.

"Now you can cook up a new colour," the woman said with a smile. Eliana put her brush in the red pot. Then she put it in the blue pot. She stirred them together on her paper. The paint turned purple! Eliana gasped. It was like magic, but her hands had done it.

She painted a purple monkey drinking a big glass of juice. The monkey looked thirsty, so she painted him a river too. "Don't touch it yet," Eliana told papa. "We have to let it dry." They sat and watched the purple monkey. They waited and waited, until the paint was dry.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: When you count, you say one number word for each object and count each object only once.
story:
Ethan sat at the little red table. His teacher, Miss Ana, put out two bowls. One bowl had apples. One bowl had grapes.

"Count them," said Miss Ana. "Then tell me which has more."

Ethan pointed at the apples. "One, two, three, four, five, six." He touched one apple two times. "Seven!"

Miss Ana smiled. "Count them again. Watch your finger. Touch each apple just once."

Ethan made a line with his finger. He pointed at each apple, one at a time. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six apples. He had counted one apple twice before. Now he got it right.

Then he counted the grapes. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven grapes.

"The grapes have more!" said Ethan. He clapped his hands.

Miss Ana laughed. "You counted so carefully, Ethan."

"Can we count the naughty crayons next?" asked Ethan. "They keep rolling off the table!"

Miss Ana put the crayons in a long line. Ethan pointed at each one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

"Ten crayons," said Ethan. "Ten is a lot!"

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: On a long drive, the family can stop at a rest stop so people can use the bathroom and stretch.
story:
Hannah sat by the train window. Rain tapped on the glass. She watched the drops slide down, down, down. "Faster, rain," she said. The rain did not listen.

Then Hannah wiggled in her seat. Her tummy felt funny. "Daddy, I need to go potty," she said. "Can the train stop at our house?" Daddy laughed a little. "The train can't stop at our house. But we can walk to the bathroom on the train." Hannah's eyes got big. "A bathroom on a train? Where?"

Daddy held her hand. They walked down the bumpy aisle. Hannah held her arms out like a bird. "Wobble, wobble," she sang. A man in a yellow hat smiled at her. At last they found the little train bathroom. It was so small! "It's a tiny potty room," said Hannah. She used it all by herself, with Daddy waiting outside.

When she came out, she felt much better. "Daddy! Now I know a secret," she said. "Trains have bathrooms hiding inside them." Daddy nodded. "And guess what else? Cars can stop at a rest stop on a long drive, so people can use the bathroom and stretch." Hannah stretched her arms up high. "Like a tall giraffe," she said. Then she pointed at the window. "Look, Daddy! The rain stopped!" The sun made a little rainbow on her seat.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Diwali, many families light small clay oil lamps called diyas.
story:
Eleanor woke up excited. Tonight was Diwali night! Mama called her to the table. "Come help, Eleanor!"

On the table were little clay cups. Eleanor counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five!" She set them in a row along the window. They were small and cool to touch. "What are these?" she asked. "These are diyas," Mama said. "They are little oil lamps."

The night came, and the sky turned dark. Papa held the match. Eleanor stood back, watching from a safe spot. Papa tipped the flame into each diya. One, two, three, four, five! The diyas began to glow. First one, then all of them!

"Again!" said Eleanor. "Count them with me!" They counted together. "One, two, three, four, five!"

The lights made the window shine. Eleanor touched the cool clay on the outside only. "Our window is full of stars," she said. The whole street had diyas too, glowing in every window, all the way down the block.
